name: The Old Government House Fig

location.address: City Botanic Gardens, on the path leading to Old Government House, Alice Street, Brisbane City QLD 4000

access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
verify_notes: Single dedicated source found (National Trust of Australia's Significant Tree Database, trusttrees.org.au), which alone does not clear the two-independent-source bar; a second, independent write-up describing this specific specimen (rather than City Botanic Gardens fig plantings generally) was not found this pass. Planted between 1864 and 1884, during Walter Hill's curatorship of the gardens (Hill was first curator, appointed 1855). Height 23m, trunk diameter 2m per National Trust record. Notable for large buttress roots. Stands on the path leading to Old Government House (Queensland's oldest public building, now part of QUT), forming a visual landmark between the two. Condition recorded as good, publicly accessible with no restriction. Coordinate is the National Trust database's own point for this individual tree, taken as tree-level (not park-level), hence confirmed.

name: The Macadamia Nut Tree

location.address: City Botanic Gardens, at the southern end of the rainforest section, Alice Street, Brisbane City QLD 4000

access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree: National Trust of Australia's Significant Tree Database and a State Library of Queensland blog post both identify this as the first cultivated Macadamia Nut Tree, planted from trials that began in 1858 by Walter Hill, the gardens' first curator, using seed brought from Gympie. Widely described elsewhere (Atlas Obscura, Australian Food Timeline) as the world's oldest known cultivated macadamia tree and the origin point of Australia's macadamia export industry; those secondary popular sources were not treated as the two required sources but corroborate the same facts. Height 17m, trunk diameter 1m per National Trust record. Good condition, unrestricted public access. Coordinate is the National Trust database's tree-level point.

name: Prince Albert's Cook Pine

location.address: City Botanic Gardens, near the George Street entrance close to Queensland Parliament House, Brisbane City QLD 4000

access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 8 minutes) or George Street bus stops nearby
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree (National Trust database and a State Library of Queensland blog post): in 1868, Prince Albert, Duke of Edinburgh (later would-be heir, not actually a king; SLQ blog mistakenly calls him 'later King Edward VII', which is wrong, Albert Edward Duke of Edinburgh was Queen Victoria's second son and never took the throne, that title belongs to his elder brother; National Trust correctly identifies him as 'Queen Victoria's son... the Duke of Edinburgh' without the throne claim, so the SLQ's royal-succession detail is not repeated as fact) planted two of a proposed avenue of six Cook Pines in front of the old Parliament House site. Only this one of the original two, and the whole avenue was never completed, so despite the species name 'avenue' in some general descriptions, only a single tree survives today, making it a genuine individual specimen rather than a blocked avenue. At approximately 45m it is the tallest tree in the gardens; trunk diameter 0.9m. Lower branches have been removed to discourage climbing. Good condition, unrestricted public access. Coordinate is the National Trust database's tree-level point.

name: The Eagle Street Fig Trees
species: White Fig and Banyan Fig (Ficus virens and Ficus benghalensis)

location.address: 118A Eagle Street, at the intersection of Eagle, Elizabeth and Creek Streets, Brisbane City QLD 4000

access: Free, a small public reserve (triangular traffic island / pocket park) open at all times
transport: Short walk from Riverside ferry terminal (about 3 minutes) or Central Station (about 8 minutes)
verify_notes: Four independent sources agree: the Queensland Heritage Register (state government, listing reference 602440, added 13 May 2004), Wikipedia's dedicated article, Brisbane City Council's own local heritage citation, and the National Trust's Significant Tree Database. Three fig trees (two White Figs, Ficus virens, and one Banyan Fig, Ficus benghalensis) planted around 1889 by Walter Hill, first curator of Brisbane's botanic gardens, on a small reserve granted by Queen Victoria (signed by Governor Sir Henry Wylie Norman, 16 May 1889) at the corner of Eagle, Elizabeth and Creek Streets. Originally gave wharf labourers and carriers shade to rest; today shades office workers in Brisbane's CBD. National Trust records: combined height 29m, canopy spread (diameter) 7m across the three trees. Condition good. This is a compact three-tree ensemble at one small, clearly bounded site (a single traffic-island reserve, not a spread-out avenue), with one obvious place to stand, so it qualifies as one collectible entry rather than a blocked avenue. Coordinate is the National Trust database's tree-level point for the site, corroborated closely by Wikipedia's stated infobox coordinates for the same heritage place.

name: The Crows Ash

location.address: City Botanic Gardens, between the formal flower garden and the river, eastern part of the gardens, Alice Street, Brisbane City QLD 4000

access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
verify_notes: Single dedicated source found (National Trust database); a second independent write-up naming this specific tree was not found this pass, though general web coverage confirms City Botanic Gardens holds native Flindersia australis specimens from a similar era. Planted 1884; the genus commemorates explorer Matthew Flinders. A separate, older Crows Ash was felled in 1826 on this same site to mark where the Moreton Bay penal settlement's government garden would be established, a distinct historical fact about the SITE rather than this living tree, kept separate to avoid implying continuity between the two trees. Height 21m, trunk diameter 1m per National Trust record. Good condition, unrestricted public access. Coordinate is the National Trust database's tree-level point.

name: The Bodhi Tree

location.address: City Botanic Gardens, just inside the Alice Street entrance, to the left of the path, Brisbane City QLD 4000

access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
verify_notes: Single dedicated source found (National Trust database); other web results describing this tree (IZI Travel audio-guide entry, a smart-guide.org walking tour listing) repeat the same claims without adding independent verification, so not counted as a second source. Planted early 1880s, said to be grown from a cutting sourced from an ancient Sri Lankan tree itself propagated from the original Bodhi Tree at Bodh Gaya, India, where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment; this lineage claim is what National Trust states but is inherently unverifiable beyond the record itself. Blessed by the 14th Dalai Lama during his 1983 visit, after attending the planting of a cutting from this tree at the University of Queensland. Height 25m, trunk diameter 3m, noted for one of the widest canopies in the gardens. Good condition, unrestricted public access. Coordinate is the National Trust database's tree-level point.

name: The Weeping Figs at Alice Street Gate

access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours

verify_notes: National Trust database describes this exact pair as standing either side of the Alice Street entrance, 'an important landmark denoting the main entrance', planted by Walter Hill; Wikipedia independently confirms the species and era only in general terms ('an avenue of weeping figs (Ficus benjamina) planted in the 1870s'), without singling out this specific entrance pair, so species and approximate decade are corroborated by a second source but the exact framing (this pair as a distinct landmark planting versus part of a longer avenue) rests on the National Trust record alone; flagged for that reason. National Trust dates planting to 1868 specifically (slightly earlier than Wikipedia's 1870s), height 40m, trunk diameter 2m, two trees. Walter Hill wrote in 1872 that the figs 'tended greatly to diminish the appearance of bareness'. Good condition, unrestricted public access. This is a compact two-tree ensemble flanking one gate, one obvious place to stand, distinct from the longer general fig avenue along the riverside boardwalk (which is not shipped as an entry, being a spread-out planting rather than a single point). Coordinate is the National Trust database's tree-level point.
